preamble: Lenition of the voiced palatal stop /ɟ/ to the palatal approximant /j/ removes the oral closure while keeping the palatal place. It is directly observable in Irish, where lenition (now an initial mutation inherited from historical intervocalic weakening) turns slender g /ɟ/ into gh /j/. Historically, the Common Slavic palatal reflex of *dj (written *ď, probably a long palatal stop [ɟː] or palatalized [dʲː]) became /j/ in Slovene, against đ in Serbo-Croatian and ž in East Slavic. Attested cases are few, so the shift is rare.

examples.note: Under lenition slender /ɟ/ becomes /j/ (broad /ɡ/ becomes /ɣ/), e.g. after the possessive 'a' 'his'. The alternation is now morphologically triggered but continues an earlier phonetic lenition of intervocalic stops.
Proto-Slavic *ď became Slovene j; compare Serbo-Croatian mèđa, Russian межа́, Czech mez, Polish miedza. The exact phonetic value of *ď (palatal stop or palatalized dental) is debated.
